analysis.one_liner: Lets agencies fire career federal workers in policy jobs without standard civil-service protections and restricts federal employee unions.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing: it was referred to the House Oversight Committee in March 2022 and died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a new employment category, "Schedule F," that reclassifies career federal workers whose jobs touch policy — including many who draft and implement regulations — so they can be hired and fired without the standard civil-service protections, such as the formal appeal process that applies to normal adverse actions. It would also make it easier to fire any federal employee for poor performance, limit grievance and arbitration rights, sharply restrict the paid time federal employees may spend doing union work, and require public reporting on union time and union contracts. The bill was referred to the House Oversight and Reform Committee and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Presidential administrations and agency political leadership gain the power to replace career staff in policy-influencing positions with people of their choosing, and to fire them quickly without the standard multi-step appeals process. Agency managers gain simpler procedures for removing poor performers. Taxpayers gain public disclosure of how much paid union time is used and what it costs.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new employment category (Schedule F) stripping job protections from career federal employees in policy-related positions, letting agencies reclassify and remove them through an expedited process.

Directs agencies to push for faster, lighter-touch firing procedures, to limit grievance arbitration over removals, and to cap the paid time employees may spend representing their union at roughly one hour per employee per year.
Requires public reporting on how much paid union time agencies grant, and makes all federal union contracts publicly available online.

analysis.who_pays: Career federal employees in policy-related jobs would bear the main cost: loss of job security and grievance protections. Federal unions would lose paid representation time and bargaining leverage, and their members would lose some workplace protections.

drawbacks.text: Schedule F removes standard firing protections from career employees in policy-related jobs, meaning any administration could more easily replace them with loyalists — the protections exist partly to keep government service professional and nonpartisan.

The bill caps union time at roughly one hour per bargaining-unit employee per year, requires advance written authorization for each use, and bars unions from using government space and equipment — measures federal unions say would make it nearly impossible to represent workers in disputes with management.

Agencies could refuse to arbitrate firings and would not have to use progressive discipline, so an employee's first mistake could lead to removal with limited recourse, even though the bill keeps a ban on prohibited personnel practices like retaliation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The stated goal — making it easier to fire genuinely poor performers — is a real problem that federal employee surveys acknowledge. But the bill's main mechanism, Schedule F, is a blunt instrument: it removes job protections from a large class of career civil servants based on their job duties, not their performance, which makes it easier for any administration to replace disloyal-seeming staff. The union-time and bargaining provisions add transparency (a genuine plus) but also stack the deck against federal unions. On balance, the accountability goals could have been pursued without dismantling the merit-based protections that keep government service professional and nonpartisan.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Oversight and Reform Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, so it expired.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 16, 2022 by Rep. Jody Hice with 11 Republican cosponsors and referred to the House Committee on Oversight and Reform.
No further action appears in the record — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
Because a bill must pass both chambers and be signed by the President to become law, the bill died when the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal employee unions and the career civil service, which kept existing firing protections and union rights; the bill's sponsors lost the chance to enact them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal unions and career civil servants

for.name: Rep. Jody B. Hice
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Accountable Feds Act on March 16, 2022.

for.name: Federal employee unions (e.g., AFGE, NTEU)
for.what_they_did: Opposed Schedule F reclassification and union-time restrictions when comparable executive actions and bills were considered, publicly campaigning against them.

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and the bill received no Democratic support; no Democrats are recorded acting on either side.

industries.note: The bill would sharply cut the paid duty time union representatives may use (capping it at about an hour per employee per year), restrict what unions can bargain over, and require agencies to renegotiate contracts to remove protections against quick firings. It also forces public disclosure of union members' union-time use by job title and compensation.

industries.industry: Career civil servants in policy-related positions
industries.note: Schedule F would strip ordinary civil-service firing protections from potentially tens of thousands of career employees whose work touches policy — including regulators and staff who draft rules — making their jobs depend on the sitting administration's approval.

The bill gives agency heads and, ultimately, the White House far more power to hire, move, and remove career staff, including the power to remove employees without the process that currently applies. Executive Order 13957, the same mechanism on a different vehicle, was widely seen as enabling a loyalist civil service.
